headline: Recommended adding public safety analysis to the City Master Plan; tabled a proposed extreme heat cooling center plan.
summary: The meeting also covered river safety signage on the Merrimack River, downtown public safety concerns, and state reimbursement for police and fire responses to State properties. Members tabled the cooling center plan so staff can gather more information.
decisions: Approved the June 18, 2026 meeting minutes unanimously.
Withdrew the motion to refer the extreme heat cooling plan directly to the City Council.
Tabled the proposed extreme heat cooling center plan by consensus while staff gather more information.
Continued the downtown public safety discussion to the September meeting, unanimously.
Recommended that the City Master Plan process include an analysis of growth and future public-safety needs; passed with no dissenting votes.

decision_titles: Public safety analysis in City Master Plan process
plain_text:
C I T Y   O F   C O N C O R D 
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
141 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
 Public Safety Advisory Board
Thursday August 20, 2026 (3:00 PM) – City Council Chambers
DRAFT Meeting Minutes
Members Present: Andrew (Drew) Biemer, Bouzned (Moe) Djabelarbi, Steve Edwards, Jessica 
Eskeland, Councilor and Chair Amanda Grady Sexton, Natch Greyes, Kate Lipman, Councilor Jim 
Schlosser, Councilor Jennifer Kretovic
City Staff Present: Fire Chief Chisholm, Interim Police Chief Barrett Moulton, Deputy Police Chief 
Casey, Police Social Worker Nicole Petrin, Police Social Worker Sara Curran, Deputy Chief Patrick 
Ofrias 
Guest: Nikki Haas, Project Director, Committee for Concord’s Plan to End Homelessness.
Minute Taker: Taryn Davidson and Councilor Amanda Grady Sexton
Councilor & Chair Amanda Grady Sexton called the meeting to order at 3:00 p.m.
Approval of Meeting Minutes
A motion was made by Councilor Kretovic and seconded by Drew Biemer to approve the minutes from 
June 18, 2026. The minutes were unanimously approved.
Extreme Heat / Cooling Center Plan
Nicole Petrin, Concord Police Social Worker, and Nikki Haas, Project Director for the Committee for 
Concord’s Plan to End Homelessness, presented a proposed community cooling plan for periods of 
extreme heat. Ms. Haas explained that Concord does not currently have a formal cooling plan for 
vulnerable residents. During a period of extreme heat over the July 4th weekend, an informal cooling 
location was established through the efforts of City Councilors and community partners. Based on that 
experience, several nonprofit organizations have expressed willingness to participate in a more formal 
plan provided that the City also participates as a partner. The organizations are not seeking financial 
assistance from the City.
The proposed cooling plan would generally mirror the City’s winter warming plan, although overnight 
accommodations would not be necessary. Cooling centers would operate during the hottest portion of the 
day, generally between approximately 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., when weather conditions meet an 
established threshold. The current proposal uses a National Weather Service heat-index threshold of 
approximately 95 degrees when conditions are considered unhealthy for vulnerable populations.
The cooling centers would be available to the general public, including older adults, families without 
adequate air conditioning, individuals experiencing homelessness, and others vulnerable to extreme heat. 
Participating organizations and service providers would assist with communicating when cooling centers 
are activated.
Ms. Haas said that community partners are asking the City to consider making municipal facilities 
available as part of the plan, including the Green Street Community Center and West Street Ward House.
C I T Y   O F   C O N C O R D 
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
241 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Councilor Kretovic suggested that Beaver Meadow Golf Course also be considered because of its 
location, public accessibility, and air-conditioned facilities. Members generally agreed that City staff 
should assess which municipal properties would be best suited for this purpose rather than limiting the 
plan to predetermined locations.
Members discussed operational and public safety considerations, including individuals subject to 
protective orders or bail conditions, registered sex offenders, interactions among individuals who may be 
prohibited from contact with one another, staffing and volunteer training, liability, and whether additional
police or emergency response resources would be necessary.
Chief Moulton explained that the Police Department routinely manages similar situations in shelters, 
social service agencies, businesses, and other public locations. Police Social Worker Petrin added that 
local service organizations frequently coordinate around protective orders and other restrictions and that 
training could be provided to cooling-center staff and volunteers regarding appropriate responses and 
when to contact law enforcement.
Members emphasized that the cooling plan should clearly communicate that the service is intended for 
anyone vulnerable to extreme heat and is not solely a homelessness initiative. Members also discussed the
importance of reviewing potential municipal liability, identifying appropriate City facilities, 
communicating with surrounding neighborhoods when locations are selected, and providing flexibility for
activation during unusual weather conditions outside the typical summer period.
An initial motion to refer the proposal directly to the City Council was discussed and subsequently 
withdrawn in favor of completing additional staff review before making a formal recommendation. By 
consensus, members agreed to table the matter while additional information is gathered regarding 
potential City locations, operational considerations, legal and liability issues, and other elements of the 
proposed plan. Ms. Haas and Ms. Petrin will work with the Chiefs and other City staff and return to the 
PSAB with a more developed proposal.
Merrimack River Safety
Councilor Kretovic raised concerns regarding water safety along the Merrimack and Contoocook Rivers 
following a recent drowning and correspondence from an individual who previously lost a loved one.
Councilor Kretovic noted that areas where waterways converge can have strong currents that may not be 
apparent from the surface and that drownings have occurred at numerous locations along the Merrimack 
River over the years. She recommended that the City consider warning signage at locations where people 
commonly access the river.
Potential locations discussed included the confluence of the Contoocook and Merrimack Rivers, Sewalls
Falls, City boat launches, the area near the Douglas N. Everett Arena, the Second Street area, and other 
commonly used fishing or swimming access points.
C I T Y   O F   C O N C O R D 
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
341 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Members discussed whether signs should be limited to locations presenting the greatest risk so that 
warnings retain their effectiveness. The Board also discussed the importance of easily understood 
messaging, potentially including multiple languages and/or universal symbols, because not all river users 
speak English as their primary language.
Chief Moulton agreed to contact the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department to determine whether 
established river-safety signage or recommended warning language is already available. Members also 
discussed reviewing FEMA or other emergency-management guidance.
Because the Merrimack River is a federal waterway, the Board discussed whether federal approvals or 
standards could apply to signage. Members noted that signs placed on City-owned land may present 
different legal considerations than signs placed within or immediately adjacent to the waterway.
Chief Moulton will consult with New Hampshire Fish and Game regarding existing signage, 
recommended language, and high-risk locations. City legal staff may be consulted as necessary regarding 
placement of signs and any applicable state or federal requirements.
Future Agenda Items
Chair Grady Sexton advised Members that the City Council has referred an item concerning tobacco use 
and potential regulation of certain tobacco-related businesses to the Public Safety Advisory Board.
Chair Grady Sexton will contact the individual who originally proposed the ordinance so that he may 
attend a future meeting and provide background information if interested/available. The Chair will also 
consult with the City Solicitor regarding Concord’s existing regulations and approaches taken by other 
municipalities. The item will be scheduled for either the September or October meeting depending upon 
the availability of the interested parties.
Downtown Public Safety
Councilor Kretovic requested that the issue of downtown public safety be placed on a future agenda. She 
reported experiencing safety concerns and hearing from downtown property owners, business owners, 
employees, and residents regarding late-night noise, aggressive or disruptive behavior, harassment, public
intoxication, individuals experiencing behavioral health crises, and other activity affecting perceptions of 
safety.
Councilor Kretovic noted concerns raised by women working downtown who walk between their 
workplaces and parked vehicles during evening hours. She suggested obtaining data to determine whether
reported experiences reflect a measurable increase in incidents and whether similar concerns exist in other
commercial areas of the City.
Chair Grady Sexton stated that she has also heard concerns from downtown residents and businesses and 
that a relatively small number of individuals appear to be responsible for a recurring portion of the 
disruptive activity.
C I T Y   O F   C O N C O R D 
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
441 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Chief Moulton discussed the Police Department’s experience responding to individuals experiencing 
mental health crises, substance misuse, and other behavioral challenges. He described recent cases in 
which the Police Department and Police Social Workers worked with providers and agencies in other 
communities to connect individuals with appropriate services.
Members discussed the limitations police may face when disruptive or concerning behavior does not 
constitute a criminal offense. Chief Moulton encouraged residents and businesses to continue reporting 
incidents so that the Department can identify trends, investigate specific concerns, and direct patrol 
resources appropriately.
Jessica Eskeland stated that, as a downtown resident and employee, she has personally observed a 
significant increase in aggressive and harassing behavior and has heard similar concerns from downtown 
business owners and other women. She emphasized that her concern relates to individuals engaging in 
threatening, aggressive, or volatile behavior and should not be equated with homelessness generally.
Members discussed the distinction between ongoing public-safety concerns and the separate obligation to 
protect human life during extreme weather emergencies. Members also noted that individuals 
experiencing homelessness may themselves be targets of aggressive or threatening behavior.
Councilor Kretovic suggested working with Intown Concord and the Greater Concord Chamber of 
Commerce on a survey of businesses to better understand the nature, locations, frequency, and timing of 
public-safety concerns. Possible responses discussed included targeted patrols, examination of existing 
ordinances, possible policy changes, and other strategies informed by collected data.
Members also discussed concerns regarding unattended shopping carts and personal belongings blocking 
sidewalks, business entrances, and accessible routes. Chief Moulton described the practical and legal 
challenges involved when the property represents an unhoused individual’s personal possessions. 
Members discussed whether additional partnerships or storage options could help address the issue while 
preserving accessibility and treating affected individuals respectfully.
Councilor Kretovic advised that she would be meeting with the President of the Greater Concord 
Chamber of Commerce and would begin a conversation regarding whether the Chamber would be 
interested in assisting with the development and distribution of a business survey.
A motion was made by Ms. Kate Lipman and seconded by Ms. Jessica Eskeland to place downtown 
public safety on the September agenda. Members unanimously agreed to continue the discussion at its 
September meeting, including consideration of a potential business survey and available public-safety 
responses.
Public Safety and the City Master Plan
Chief Chisholm raised the upcoming City Master Plan process and recommended that public safety be 
specifically incorporated into the planning effort. He noted that prior master planning efforts have not 
necessarily included a detailed analysis of how anticipated residential and commercial growth will affect 
police, fire, and other public-safety services.
C I T Y   O F   C O N C O R D 
New Hampshire’s Main Street™
541 Green Street • Concord, NH  03301 • (603) 225-8500
Members discussed the importance of evaluating projected growth alongside future public-safety needs, 
including personnel, apparatus, facilities, service demand, station locations, response volumes, and other 
infrastructure needs. Members agreed that incorporating measurable data, best practices, and projected 
demand into the Master Plan would provide a stronger basis for future public-safety investments.
Members also discussed participating directly in the Master Plan’s community-engagement process and 
reviewing the existing engagement schedule to determine whether an additional Public Safety Advisory 
Board session would be beneficial.
Ms. Kate Lipman moved that the Board issue a report recommending that the City’s Master Plan process 
include an analysis coordinating anticipated City growth with future public-safety needs, including 
personnel, apparatus, facilities, potential future facility locations, service capacity, and community 
engagement. The motion was seconded by Mr. Drew Biemer. The motion passed with no dissenting votes.
The recommendation will be transmitted to the City Council and the appropriate Master Plan/Planning 
Board process and members of the PSAB are encouraged to attend upcoming Master Plan meetings.
State Funding for Police and Fire Responses to State Properties
Councilor Kretovic provided a brief follow-up regarding prior discussions about State reimbursement to 
the City for police and fire responses involving State properties. Councilor Kretovic reported that she and 
Chief Chisholm are working to compile supporting service-calls and cost data develop, and that 
legislation may be filed to increase State funding based upon the current level and cost of public-safety 
services Concord provides to State facilities.
Member Comment
Ms. Jessica Eskeland addressed comments made by the Ward 5 City Councilor at a recent City Council 
meeting regarding social districts. Ms. Eskeland stated that the Ward 5 Councilor had made allegations 
regarding her participation in discussions on the topic of social districts. Ms. Eskeland stated that 
although her firm represents a beverage distributor, the client did not communicate with her regarding the 
social district proposal, had no involvement in the issue, and had no interest in its outcome. She stated 
that she takes her ethical responsibilities, integrity, and transparency seriously and would have recused 
herself had a conflict existed.
Ms. Eskeland expressed concern that publicly questioning the integrity of volunteer board members 
without a factual basis could discourage residents from serving on City boards and committees.
Chair Grady Sexton thanked Eskeland for her service and expressed appreciation for the time and 
commitment of all Board members.
Adjournment
A motion to adjourn was made by Councilor Kretovic and seconded by Ms. Kate Lipman. The motion 
passed unanimously. Chair Grady Sexton adjourned the meeting at 4:21 p.m.
